title.en: The Birth of Shango in Nupeland

region.en: Oyo-Ile and Nupeland (symbolic pin: Old Oyo, Shango's royal seat)
region.zh: 舊奧約與努佩地帶（象徵定位：尚戈的王都舊奧約）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: The Ibadan tellers make Oranjan (Oranyan) Shango's father: a great warrior who conquered and lost Ife, went to Okuland and married Yemodia, a woman of Takpa (Nupe) blood, taking no second wife; Shango was born in Nupeland and ruled at Old Ojo. The coast version says simply that Shango was the mightiest of the sons the All-Mother Yemaya bore at Ife — first royal ruler of the country, whose posterity still give Yoruba its kings.
summary.zh: 伊巴丹的講述者以奧蘭揚為尚戈之父：這位大戰士曾攻克伊費復又失守，遠行奧庫之地娶塔卡（努佩）血統的耶莫迪亞為妻，終生不二色。尚戈生於努佩之地，都於舊奧約。海濱版本則直言：尚戈乃是太母耶莫雅在伊費所生諸子中最強者——本國第一位君王，其子孫至今擁立約魯巴的國王。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the royal genealogy tying the Alaafin line to Shango, recorded 1910-12 by Frobenius. Two competing origin versions (Ife theogony vs Nupeland genealogy) are preserved side by side as the source states.

passages.text: What was told in Ibadan was this: Oranjan was Shango's sire. His mother was Yemodia; Laro was Oranjan's father, and Yemodia's Aussi. Oranjan was a great warrior in Yoruba. He once conquered Ilife (Ife), but was driven forth again. He went to Okuland; there lived Yemodia, who was of Takpa (or Nupe) blood. There Oranjan married Yemodia. She was his only wife, and he took no second, as negroes do. Then Shango was born in Nupeland. Oranjan became king in Oduma-ushe. But Shango ruled in Old-Ojo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The myths on the Coast relate that Shango was the mightiest man born of the All-Mother, Yemaya, in Ife — as powerful, as warlike and as mighty a God as was ever created in the minds of a nation striving for self-expression in great ideas. This country's first royal ruler sprang, as its people believe, from his loins; his posterity still have the right to give the country its kings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango Forces His Two Captains to Fight

region.en: Old Oyo, Nigeria (the court where the king demanded endless war)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約（國王索戰不休的宮廷）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Passionately devoted to war, King Shango sent his two high officers, Mokwa and Timi, out day after day to raze towns in his name — and spat fire at them for not doing more. When the two complained together, he constrained them to fight each other; Mokwa at length slew his friend Timi, then declared he would kill the king too. Shango bade him call the people; the assembly decreed that Shango must depart the land within five days, and he went of his own free will.
summary.zh: 尚戈王酷嗜征伐，日日遣兩員重臣莫克瓦與蒂米出兵毀城，稍有不力便口噴烈焰。二人同來陳情，王竟逼他們自相殘殺；莫克瓦終手刃摯友蒂米，繼而宣言亦要誅王。尚戈命他召集群眾公斷；民意裁定：五日之內，王必須離境。尚戈遂自願出走。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the expulsion of the war-king that precedes his deification (Frobenius 1913). Mokwa and Timi survive as the names of real Yoruba chieftaincies (Mokwa, Timi of Ede).

passages.text: When Shango was King of Ojo he had two Ironse (high officers or courtiers). One was Mokwa (or Mogba), the other Timi Agbala-Olofa-no. Shango was passionately devoted to war, so he often sent Timi and Mokwa out, who waged war and destroyed towns in his name. He was so warlike that at last the people of Ojo assembled, saying: "Our king wastes all the country round; we desire a ruler who will give us, not slaves, but meat." They sent an embassy to Shango: "Thou hast been king; thou wert too strict; thou wert too cruel; wicked thou art. Therefore, thou shalt cease to be king."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mokwa related: "Shango sent forth Timi and Mokwa every day to wage war. He said at morn, 'Go, do thus and thus!' At night we came, saying, 'It has been done!' Shango answered: 'Nay, I am not content. To-morrow ye must forth, and do yet more.' Each day we went; Shango spat fire and bade us go. One day we two came unto him, saying: 'Thou dost naught but vomit flames from forth thy mouth. Enough!' Then said Shango: 'Ye are come one with the other to complain of me. But, now, I will constrain ye that ye fight one with another.' So we fought, for we were compelled. I, Mokwa, slew Timi at length. Timi, Mokwa's friend, lay dead. Then Mokwa spake to Shango: 'Thou forcedst me to slay this man. He was not mine enemy. Therefore I will slay thee also.' Shango spake: 'How? Thou wouldst slay me? Call the people together in the city; hearken unto them. And mark thou what cometh to pass.'"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mokwa called the people and spoke unto them thus: "Each day Royal Shango sent Mokwa and Timi forth to raze the cities and to slay. They waxed faint. They complained. Shango constrained them to contend. They contended. Mokwa slew Timi. Mokwa said to Shango the king: 'Now will I kill thee also.' Shango said: 'Call the people.' I, Mokwa, did so. Ye are here; say ye what shall be done!" The people cried: "Shango must depart the land within five days." Thus they spake to Shango. He took a rope and went away into the forest. This is how it came to pass. It is true that none could slay Shango. He departed of his own free-will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: "What Mokwa Can, I Can": Shango Burns and Rises
title.zh: 「莫克瓦能者吾亦能」——尚戈焚而復生

region.en: Old Oyo, Nigeria (the pyre in the middle of the road)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約（大道中央的柴堆）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: In one account of Shango's passing, the king orders a wood-pile twenty-four feet high piled in the middle of the road, drenched with palm kernels and oil, and sets the torch — then throws his captain Mokwa upon it. Mokwa is consumed, and comes to life again. Astonished, Shango declares, "What Mokwa can, I can. But I will not be a man, I will become an Orisha!" and hangs himself in the bush wearing his skin apron and sixteen cowries; he becomes an Orisha and ascends into heaven, the cowries sacred to him ever after, and Mokwa becomes his first priest.
summary.zh: 一說尚戈命人在大道中央堆起二十四尺高的柴堆，澆以棕櫚油與果仁，親自點火——隨即把部將莫克瓦擲上火堆。莫克瓦焚盡，竟又復活。尚戈大驚，宣言：「莫克瓦能者，吾亦能。然吾不願再為人，吾將成神！」遂披皮裙、佩十六貝幣，入林自縊；自此他成為奧里莎，直上青天。貝幣從此為其聖物，莫克瓦則成其首位祭司。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the death-and-apotheosis of Shango (Frobenius 1913). Strong cross-tradition fit for the death-and-resurrection cluster. Cross-refs: egyptian-osiris-cycle, norse-ragnarok (renewal), christian-passion-resurrection.

passages.text: Once, when Mokwa was at war, Shango sent word to the people of Ojo to make a wood-pile not less than twenty-four feet high in the middle of the road. Palm kernels and palm oil were to be poured upon it. Everything was prepared and Shango applied the torch. When the blaze was at its height, Shango threw Mokwa on top of it. But when Mokwa had been consumed he came to life again. Shango was greatly astonished. He said: "What Mokwa can, I can. But I will not be a man, I will become an Orisha!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon he took his apron, which was made of skin, and sixteen cowrie shells. He went into the bush and hanged himself upon an Anjo tree. So Shango became an Orisha and ascended into heaven; the cowries were sacred to him, for one throws them for him (oracle), and thus Mokwa became his first priest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

region.en: Old Oyo and Kushi, Nigeria (the Anjo tree on the road to Kushi)
region.zh: 舊奧約與庫希（往庫希路旁的自縊之樹）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango, born in Takpaland, set his people a threefold law: first truth — lying he loathed; second, none should poison another; third, none should steal or break the bounds of mine and thine. Whoso offends against this triple commandment, Shango — now an Orisha — will slay: he appears in the Ara, the thunderstorm, and kills with the stone Ara-dung, the meteorite. As a living king he was an Oni-Sheggo, a sorcerer; his two deputies were the good Ossenj and the wicked Edju, and setting out to meet Edju at Kushi he hanged himself on an Anjo tree by the way, then went up into the sky by a chain.
summary.zh: 生於塔卡之地的尚戈為民立三誡：一曰真——謊言為其所憎；二曰無相鴆；三曰勿竊、勿逾你我之界。凡犯此三誡者，已成神的尚戈必誅之：他顯形於「阿剌」雷暴之中，以「阿剌敦」隕石殺人。生前他是行蠱的「奧尼謝戈」；麾下二將，善者奧森傑，惡者埃茹。他往庫希去會埃茹，途中在一棵安喬樹上自縊，而後循鐵鏈升天。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the ethical commandments attached to Shango's cult (Frobenius 1913) — an unusual theomorphic law-code. Recorded 1910-12.

passages.text: Shango the King was born in Takpaland. The first thing he demanded was the truth; lying he loathed. Nor, secondly, was it his will that people should poison each other. Thirdly, he set his face against the Yorubans stealing from each other and going into each other's houses in the cities and disregarding the laws of meum and tuum. If any offend against this triple commandment, Shango, who is to-day an Orisha, will slay him. Shango will appear in the Ara, the Thunderstorm, and he kills with the stone Ara-dung, or our meteorite.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: While Shango lived he was an Oni-Sheggo and ascended to heaven by a chain. He killed himself on high, and this was the way of it: in war he had two Enondje (deputies or envoys), one of whom was very good, the other very evil. The bad one was Edju, the good one Ossenj. One day Ossenj said to the King, then dwelling in Ojo, that Edju had told him Shango could not return. Now, Edju was then in Kushi in Yorubaland. So Shango set out to meet him, but hanged himself on his way on an Anjo tree. This is why the people still appeal to him always as Obaku-su! Then he went up into the sky by a chain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Shango on the Storm-Ram, and the Stones in the Fields
title.zh: 雷羊背上的尚戈與田中石斧

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the fields where thunderbolts are found)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（象徵定位：拾得雷石的田間）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango rides the storm: "When Shango rides across the heavens in a storm, he stands upon the backs of goats, and his favourite food is ram." Stone axes dug from the fields are his missiles — a peasant who finds one sets it on the god's altar and prays for rains and plenty; and his effigies show two dynasties, the elder Taba Shango masked as a ram over his fire-medicine, the later Mesi Shango always on horseback.
summary.zh: 尚戈乘風而行：「雷暴橫天之時，尚戈足踏群羊之背；公綿羊是他至愛的祭饌。」田中掘得的石斧即其飛石——農夫拾得便供上神壇，禱求風調雨順、五穀豐登。其神像分兩朝：古老的塔巴尚戈以公羊假面覆其火藥秘藏；後起的梅西尚戈則永遠跨騎戰馬。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the thunderbolt-stone (celt) cult is well attested across the Sudan (Frobenius 1913). The sun-ram parallel (Ammon) is Frobenius's comparison; tagged sun-capture only as interpretive cluster link.

passages.text: On the last day of my stay in Ibadan I was looking in the yard at my horse, which was fresh and lustily pawing the ground. An old Yoruban looked at it admiringly and compared the freshness of my steed to the vigour of Shango's rams. The old fellow, on further questioning, said: "When Shango rides across the heavens in a storm, he stands upon the backs of goats and his favourite food is ram." Shango's effigy in Ojo is a ram's mask which conceals his holy, light-giving magic.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The symbols of divinity are almost always present on all royal gates as well as on the portals leading to temples: little stone axes, the missiles of the God; the wedges decorated with stone hatchet heads, the Ose-Shango; the long-handled Shango-rattles; and the great leathern wallets, or Laba-Shango. There is a plethora of emblems set up in the temples and on country roadsides, which always express the twofold prayer to the God to send the blessed and fertilizing rain without the loss of human life by strokes of lightning. But when the peasant finds an ancient stone axe in his fields, he carefully picks it up and puts it among his produce or upon the altar of the God as the symbol and instrument of his might, praying him to bless his crops and send him rains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the royal house said that most certainly the Alafins derived their descent from Shango the Thunder God, but that there had been two different Shangos: the elder was the Takpa or Taba, and the other the Mesi, Shango. The name of the former shows that he came from Nupeland, but the latter from Borgu, where Mesi, in all the old histories and tales, is the name of the King. Legend maintains that the Mesi Shango dynasty was conquered and driven out by reason of the Taba Shango's renewed accession to power. Mesi Shango are said to be always represented on horseback; Shango Taba, however, was always shown in the guise of a ram. There are two such ram-masks in Ojo, forming the lid of a casket which had held the fire medicine of this God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire-Dance of Shango: Ear, Tongue and Eye Restored
title.zh: 尚戈踏火之舞——耳舌眼復生

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (the fire-pot carried in the great festival)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（大祭中頂在頭上的火壇）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: At Shango's great festival the fire-dancer carries a ritual pot of the Jena, Shango's fire, on his head. Charged with magic, he works miracles: stoops and picks up a handful of earth that turns to salt or cowries; cuts off an ear which the sacred flame replaces; removes his tongue and it grows again; plucks out an eye, burns it, swallows it — and sees with the recreated optic as distinctly as ever. But the performer must first have made the power of Ossenj his own, for no miracles without Ossenj. At the solstice every hearth is extinguished and each family carries home a brand from Shango's fire: the birth of the new year.
summary.zh: 尚戈大祭之日，踏火者頭頂盛著「耶納」聖火的祭壇。他借符力顯奇：俯身拾土，土化為鹽或貝幣；割下一耳，聖火為之再生；扯下舌頭，復又長回；剜出一眼，燒之吞下——新生的眼卻看得分明如昔。但行奇蹟者必先得「奧森傑」之力——無奧森傑則無奇蹟。冬至之祭，萬火俱熄，家家自尚戈聖火取一根火種而歸：新年由此誕生。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Shango fire-dance (Frobenius 1913) — fire-walking with the Ose-Shango remains part of Shango devotional performance. Recorded 1910-12; described as the source states it.

passages.text: One of the most interesting of the cult's offerings is the fire-dance. The dancer has a ritual pot (Adjeri) or basket (Agba) on his head, in which burns the Jena, or Shango fire. He at first takes an apparently reckless turn or two, which completely loads him up with magic forces, enabling him to perform miracles with ease. He can stoop and pick up a handful of earth which turns into salt or cowrie-shells. He can cut off one of his ears, which the sacred flame on his head will replace. He can remove his tongue from his neck, and the sacred flame will make it grow again there. He pulls out an eye, burns it and swallows it; but the fire-dancer's optic will be recreated and he will see with it again as distinctly as ever. This kind of dance is carried out at the great seven-day festival and the Batta drummer drums to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Through it all we must not forget that these people believe that the great god Shango himself could not do these marvellous things without help: the fire-dancer has first to make the power of Ossenj his own. The fire-pot is brought back to the Shango priest at the close of this magical day; and when it is relighted in the following year the Shaman will well knead the head and the body of the dancer, so as to shield him from the hurt of the fire. No miracles without Ossenj! Should this festival be held at the time of the solstice, fires are everywhere extinguished and every one takes a brand from the burning fire of Shango to his home. Then this is the birth of the New Year for the ministers of Shango.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Elogun-Shango: The God Seizes a Dancer
title.zh: 埃洛貢尚戈——神附舞者之身

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (the temple court and the road to the Bale's house)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（廟庭與通往巴萊宅邸的街路）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango descends quite unexpectedly on some dancer's head: the inspired one rushes to the temple chamber, seizes the carved Ose-Shango club or the holy rattle, and capers before the crowd — and everyone agrees one possessed by Shango dances differently from ordinary folk. The Batta drummer joins; the whole procession follows the dancer home, and the Bale takes off his own cap and lays it on the ground before the deity in human shape — the utmost homage a man whose forehead never bends to earth can be expected to pay. One man told Frobenius he woke to find all doing him obeisance, not remembering what had happened.
summary.zh: 尚戈突降於某舞者之頂：被附身者狂奔入廟，抓起雕工精美的奧謝尚戈杖或聖鈴，在眾人前手舞足蹈——人皆言，被尚戈附身者舞姿迥異常人。鼓師擊巴塔鼓相隨，全城尾隨舞者歸宅；巴萊（村長）竟摘下自家冠帽置於神附之身前的地上——額不觸地之人所能致的最高敬禮。一名經歷者自述：醒來方知眾人皆向自己跪拜，事前渾然不覺。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; orisha-possession (Elogun-Shango) remains central to Shango devotion in Yorubaland and the diaspora. Frobenius records a first-person account; presented as archival testimony.

passages.text: The stories told by those who have assisted at these festivals and exaltations of feeling sound very much the same. Shango descends quite unexpectedly upon some man or woman dancer's head. The inspirationist rushes madly to the Banga, seizes an Ose-Shango, a beautifully carved club, or a Shere-Shango, that is, the holy rattle. This individual begins to caper before the others. The afflatus is patent. All agree in this: a being possessed by Shango or any other Orisha dances quite differently from ordinary folk. The beater of the sacred Batta drum joins the dancer, and they leave the temple court with all the rest at their heels. He dances to his own house, followed by them all, and then everyone well knows that this person is a friend, a darling of Shango's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Arrived at his home, the God-favoured one will provide sacrificial rams, cowries, kola and drink for the commune, so that they all may know and experience the gratitude he feels. In Ibadan there is one road always taken by these temporary inspired ones: it leads to the house of the Bale in office. The dance goes on in the courtyard, and the master of the house will certainly honour this dancer by the grace of God: he takes off his Bale cap, the Akitajo, and lays it on the ground before the deity in human shape — the utmost homage which so great a man, whose forehead never bends to earth unless the headsman's glaive parts head from trunk, can be expected to pay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A highly-esteemed person told how, some years ago, Shango had made him his mouthpiece to the people. He had danced with the rest and danced very swiftly; someone asked whether there was likely to be an Elogun-Shango (a God-inspired one) that day, and somebody said you never could tell — not even the augur, nor even the person himself, for it might happen to anyone. Then he had felt very strange; he was compelled to rush to the temple chamber and snatch up an Ose-Shango. What came next he was unable to say; but he felt very jolly and drank a lot that evening and went to sleep drunk. Everyone did him obeisance next day, and that was the first time he heard what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Oya Sweeps the Road Before the Thunderer

region.en: River Niger country (symbolic pin: the storm-wind preceding the storm over the Niger)
region.zh: 奈及利亞尼日河鄉（象徵定位：雷暴前掃過尼日河的疾風）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: In the Ibadan version Shango's only wife was Oja, the lake — a mighty huntress of leopard, antelope and elephant with her younger brother at her side; after Shango's marriage and self-sought death she transformed herself into the River Niger. An Ilesha man added that she had first been married to Ogun, who was so evil she ran away to Shango; she still performs her wifely duty and sweeps the road before him clean in the wind that heralds the storm, ranks as mother of Shango's children and thus of the Alafins, and abides in the sky with him. Her priests and priestesses always sacrifice sheep, never goats; goats are forbidden to be killed or eaten.
summary.zh: 伊巴丹版本中，尚戈唯一的妻子是湖澤女神奧雅——豹鹿象皆其所獵的巾幗獵手，幼弟常隨左右。尚戈自縊之後，她化身為尼日河。伊萊沙的講述者又說：她原嫁暴戾的奧貢，不堪其惡而逃奔尚戈；至今雷暴之前的疾風，正是她為夫君清道；她是尚戈諸子、亦即歷代阿勞芬王的母親，與夫同住天界。其祭司只獻羊，永不殺羊、永不食羊。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Oya (Oja) as the Niger and storm-wind, recorded 1910-12. Goat taboo in Oya cult reported by Frobenius.

passages.text: In the Ibadan version, Shango's only wife was Oja, the lake. Now, Oja was a mighty huntress and followed the chase with exceeding skill; she hunted all the wild things in the bush, leopards, antelopes and elephants, and had a younger brother, her constant companion on the trail. After Shango's marriage and suicide, Oja transformed herself into the River Niger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: An Ilesha man supplied this supplement: Oja was Shango's spouse; she still performs her wifely duty and sweeps the road before him clean. She had before been married to Ogun, who was so evil that she ran away to Shango, married and lived with him. Oja ranks as the mother of Shango's children and thus of the Alafins, the blood-royal of Ojo. In her present form she abides in the sky with Shango. When the festival of Oja is at hand, i.e., in December or January, many people go to the river and make her offerings. Oja's priests and priestesses always sacrifice sheep, but never goats to this deity: goats are forbidden to be killed or eaten.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Nini, the Son of Shango, Is No More

region.en: Old Oyo, Nigeria (the Batta drum sounding the death proclamation)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約（巴塔鼓宣告死訊之地）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XI

summary.en: Shango had a son, Nini, killed in one of his many wars. The drum, Batta, was beaten and proclamation made: "Nini, the son of Shango, is no more!" And since that time Nini's death is a topic forbidden at the dying hour of a Shango descendant — a prohibition tied, it is said, to some magical spell whose quintessence could not be grasped even by Frobenius.
summary.zh: 尚戈有一子名尼尼，歿於連年征戰之一。巴塔大鼓擂響，宣告於眾：「尚戈之子尼尼已逝！」自那時起，凡尚戈子孫臨終之際，「尼尼之死」便成禁忌之語——相傳此事繫於某種咒法，其真義連記錄者也未能參透。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; a death-taboo etiology inside the Shango cycle (Frobenius 1913).

passages.text: There is a wonderful story of Nini's death. For Shango, namely, had a son, called Nini, killed in one of his many wars. The drum, Batta, was beaten and proclamation made: "Nini, the son of Shango, is no more!" And since that time, Nini's death is a topic forbidden at the dying hour of a Shango descendant. I never could grasp this legend's quintessence, which is said to relate to some magical spell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XI (1913); not verbatim.
